name: "Killing Your Internship" — Consulting Internship Tips
next_step: Send networking messages in weeks 1-2 from people you interviewed with, wait until you have firm email. Meet with everyone on team ASAP. Prioritize manager relationship.
notes:
Panel: "Killing Your Internship" — Consulting Internship Tips
Panelists: Jose Magana (Deloitte LA), Nathan Perez (Bain Boston), Ramya Srinivasan (McKinsey NYC), Wenny Zhang (Kearney NYC)

Before You Start

Do Excel/PPT technical prep
Don't send networking messages weeks 1–2; wait until you have a firm email; reach out to people you interviewed with
Jose: cold-reach your manager 2x before day one

First Case / Hitting the Ground Running

Ask your manager: "What's the single most important thing to know/do?" and confirm priorities regularly
Ask your manager: "What's your preferred method for me to ask questions?"
Have a roles/responsibilities discussion early — who's note-taking, what's your priority on the case
Learn the 3 types of acronyms: industry, firm, and client-specific
Leverage your analyst — they have tons of firm/team context
Nathan: create a question list for peers; take lots of notes; be early to everything
Jose: volunteer for everything, including low-hanging fruit — builds capital
Wenny: be proactive, anticipate needs
Sharon: ownership mentality — don't wait to be told every step
Write daily tasks on paper

Feedback

Set up informal weekly check-ins with your manager
Also set up 15–20 min weekly with your analyst and ask them for feedback
Go into every meeting armed with a perspective; ask "how do you think it's going?"
Log feedback in a notebook
Prepare for midterm/final reviews with a list of accomplishments, growth areas, and things still improving
Have a mentor outside your case for unbiased cross-case perspective
Nick: two levels of feedback — high-level/strategic AND tactical; don't repeat tactical errors; new mistakes are fine
Sharon (BCG): don't be surprised by anything in your midterm slide — have evidence of improvements ready
If only getting positive feedback, explicitly ask for constructive

Return Offer

Jose's top 3 priorities: (1) perform well, (2) make a great impression, (3) get the return offer
Trust that they want you to succeed — feedback comes from a good place
Show enthusiasm consistently — firms notice (especially Kearney)
Ramya: even when told "you should chill," keep pushing to improve
Sharon: stay receptive to feedback with a positive attitude

Closing Strong

Be proactive about transferring materials to whoever picks up the work
Network for future staffing considerations
Attend all social events; connect with your intern cohort
Nathan: don't lead with a "corporate persona" — slowly let your real self show
Ramya: go to dinner/drinks with EMs; keep connections warm heading into 2nd year

Support Network

Build genuine friendships with EMs and analysts — huge for personal support
Have a "vent buddy" at another firm or outside the industry
Know who to go to for what (SOM alumni network within firm, intern cohort group chat)
Don't have a competitive relationship with other interns — ask them "dumb" questions freely

name: Abdul-Razak Zacharriah
next_step: Follow up on housing innovation topics discussed; explore connections around zoning reform and ADU policy
notes:
Notes from Yale Innovation Summit on 5/27. Session focused on fixing zoning and housing innovation. Multiple attendees: Peter Harrison (Rezoning Plan), Nick Callegari / Venstruct (startup), Kasey Lafton (LISC CT), Abdul-Razer Zaharrah (City Plan), Missy Norcula (economist/philanthropist).

80% housing vacancy rate, 64% 1-2 units. Class A strain on builders. Vision 2034: eliminate parking minimums, no cars, biking and changing culture, where is this land? Zoning toward low-income numbers. How can this work and increase fair share access.

LITC - utility, more timber. Updates: short-term vs long-term $. Goes through IRS (not HUD).

Public-private partnerships: 3-4 units. Naturally occurring low-income housing, no subsidies. 40% affordable or luxury. Attention, policy, subsidies — encourage filling gap: 60-120 units.

PREM: comfort level. See who starts in communities. Aesthetic, can be approved. Construction not changing — most cities by 2031 but next gen not entering construction. Labor - jobs. Robot - approved plans. Stream system for inspectors. Zoning + aesthetics + jobs.

'Slip form' — smooth walls, construction 'dignified.' We have manufacturer proof pictures, becoming short updates. Weekly calls with local community and inspectors. Less attention but better quicker to approve.

Missy: Bay Area founder, $50M/yr. 'Society's best capital' — trying not to make money, do what you can see. That's innovation for them.
- Housing Accelerator Fund — short-term price loans to do. Schools/pressure, the public.
- Turner Center — housing policy, second home unlocking private $.
- Catalyst Input Fund — see Joe. Ship loaning → affordable housing. Bridge: $10M to unlock 160 units in area. Only 3% schools. Only philanthropy can fill gap.
- Family formation → changing return.
- Family Foundation → only to C-3. Loans only when together can give to for-profit, low ROI.

ADUs — gentle density in single-family suburban. 2% zoned as multi-family — in CT. 67% CT land is single-family zoned. → ADU: bridge gap.
Barriers to streamlining: aging in community, downsize but live in area, familiar with. Move into ADU, rent main.

Who benefits from more? It grows capital — government, philanthropic, cause solving, host community, startups, owners. The main way to solving communal problems.

ADU is not a right — little rent to affordable, large regulatory. Often solving for family to move in. 'Regularize it' — don't call it out, it's in many ways don't call attention to it.

→ Remove parking minimums.
